content: The use of vitamin C, also known as ascorbic acid, for preventing and treating the common cold has been a topic of debate for the past 70 years. Researchers aimed to determine whether vitamin C could reduce the incidence, duration, or severity of the common cold when taken either as a daily supplement or as a treatment initiated at the onset of symptoms. To investigate this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, LILACS, and the Web of Science, was conducted up to November 2012. Additionally, clinical trial registries such as the U.S. National Institutes of Health trials register and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) were searched. Only placebo-controlled trials using a minimum daily dose of 0.2 grams of vitamin C were included in the analysis. Data from the studies were independently extracted by two reviewers. The incidence of colds during regular supplementation was defined as the proportion of participants who experienced one or more colds during the study period. The duration of colds was measured as the average number of days participants were ill during cold episodes. The meta-analysis included 29 trial comparisons involving a total of 11,306 participants. In trials conducted in the general population (10,708 participants), the pooled risk ratio (RR) for developing a cold while taking vitamin C regularly was 0.97 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.94 to 1.00), indicating no significant reduction in cold incidence. However, in five trials involving 598 individuals exposed to extreme physical stress, such as marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers in subarctic conditions, the pooled RR was 0.48 (95% CI: 0.35 to 0.64), suggesting a significant reduction in cold incidence in these groups. Thirty-one comparisons assessed the effect of regular vitamin C supplementation on the duration of colds, encompassing 9,745 cold episodes. In adults, regular vitamin C use reduced the duration of colds by 8% (95% CI: 3% to 12%), while in children, the reduction was 14% (95% CI: 7% to 21%). Higher doses of 1 to 2 grams per day in children shortened cold duration by 18%. Regular vitamin C supplementation also reduced the severity of cold symptoms. Seven comparisons evaluated the therapeutic use of vitamin C (3,249 cold episodes), where vitamin C was administered after the onset of symptoms. These trials did not demonstrate a consistent effect on either the duration or severity of colds. Most of the included trials were randomized, double-blind studies. Excluding trials that were not randomized or double-blind did not alter the overall conclusions. The authors concluded that routine vitamin C supplementation does not reduce the incidence of colds in the general population and is therefore not justified for this purpose. However, vitamin C may be beneficial for individuals exposed to short periods of intense physical exertion. Regular supplementation has been shown to reduce the duration and severity of colds, but this effect was not observed in therapeutic trials where vitamin C was taken after symptoms began. Given the consistent findings from regular supplementation studies, along with the low cost and safety of vitamin C, it may be worth considering for individuals to test its therapeutic effects on a case-by-case basis. Further randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on the therapeutic use of vitamin C are warranted.
